body.heading: Names for humans, numbers for machines
paragraphs: Computers on the internet reach each other using numerical addresses called IP addresses. Numbers work well for machines and badly for human memory, so we mostly use names instead — the words you type into a browser's address bar.

The Domain Name System, DNS, is the service that translates a name into the matching numerical address. It is often described as the internet's phone book, and almost every visit to a website begins with a DNS question.

body.heading: Asking around, in milliseconds
paragraphs: When you type a name, your device first checks whether it already knows the answer from a recent lookup. If not, it asks a resolver, usually run by your internet provider or another service, which goes looking on your behalf.

The resolver may ask a chain of servers: one that knows about endings like .com, then the organisation's own name server, which gives the final answer. The whole conversation usually finishes in a small fraction of a second, and the answer is remembered for a while to save repeating it.

body.heading: Why DNS matters more than it looks
paragraphs: Because DNS sits at the start of almost everything online, its design choices matter. If a name is typed slightly wrong, or a record is changed, visitors can end up somewhere unexpected — which is why checking web addresses carefully is good advice.

DNS was designed in the 1980s, when the internet was a small, trusting research network. It has been extended and made more secure ever since, but its basic idea — ask around until someone authoritative answers — still runs the modern web.

takeaway: DNS is the internet's translator: it turns the names humans remember into the numerical IP addresses computers need, usually in a fraction of a second.
